subject: riotInterceptor
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: corporate riot-control interceptor with a water cannon and neon light bars.
Style: Cyberpunk 2077.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single large TypeScript module targeting 180-340 parts, 5-12 textures, and roughly 700-1100 lines, aiming for something manageable yet rich since I can't test it directly. I'm sketching out a design for a heavy armored riot-control interceptor vehicle with a wide wheelbase.

I'm figuring out the proportions — roughly 6.2m long, 2.4m wide, 2.9m tall — with a roof-mounted water cannon turret, neon light bars, and corporate decal-style livery mixing cyberpunk colors like yellow, cyan, and magenta against dark navy. I'm working out the skeleton structure with wheel joints across multiple axles, steerable front wheels, a turret with yaw/pitch/nozzle joints, and hinged doors, plus helper functions for boxes, part creation, and neon glow effects. Now I'm thinking through how to construct the main hull body in a blocky, stylized way.

Writing paint and livery code...

I'm working out the truck's hull geometry: three axles spaced along a 6.6m body length, wheel radius and width sized to tuck into arches, with the body around 2.3m wide. I'm realizing the wheel arches need to be cut into the side outline itself as concave notches approximating a semicircle, rather than treated as separate geometry.

I also need to handle the fact that an arch cutout goes all the way through the body thickness, so I'm planning dark wheel-well liner boxes inside the arches to block the see-through gap and make it look like a real recessed wheel well rather than a hole.

Actually, simpler approach: raise the body bottom and let the wheels protrude outward with fender flare boxes above them, overlapping the body sides slightly — more robust than cutting arches into the body geometry.

I'll go with armored fender boxes instead, using an outline with arch notches in the z,y plane, treating x as the forward direction. I'm working out wheel radius, axle positions, and overall spacing — roughly three axles with a front near z=2.1, mid around z=-1.0, and rear near z=-2.35, keeping the nose extending to z=3.5 and the rear overhang to z=-3.4.

Checking the tandem rear axle spacing more carefully, I settle on axle positions at z = 2.1, -0.9, and -2.3, then work out the arch half-widths to avoid overlap between the two rear wheel arches, adjusting the half-width down to 0.68 so the arches fit cleanly without clipping into each other.

Since the two rear arches end up nearly touching anyway, I merge them into one long continuous notch spanning roughly -2.98 to -0.22 at y=1.25, which better represents a tandem bogie slot and simplifies the geometry. Now I'm tracing the body outline coordinates from the rear bottom corner forward along the underside, laying out the (z,y) points for the bumper and wheel well region.

Still writing outline points...

Behind the cab, the rear compartment becomes the taller water tank housing, roof at 2.95 extending back to a vertical rear face around z=-3.45 -- essentially the tank body sitting higher than the cab roof.

Checking the barrel length against the light bar position, it clears fine extending to z=2.3. I'm reconsidering the rear roof tank placement — a cylinder centered at y=3.0 with radius .6 spanning z=-3.2 to -0.7 with saddle mounts, bringing total height to around 3.6-3.9m, which is a bit tall compared to real armored trucks at ~3.3m but I'll keep it close.

So I'm trimming down: cab roof at 2.55, rear box at 2.2, tank cylinder centered at 2.75 with radius .5 topping at 3.25, and the turret pivot sitting over the cab roof with a short pedestal, landing total height near 3.4 — that works better. Now I'm tracing the profile outline from front to back: nose bottom and top, a short hood sloping up to the windscreen base, then a flat cab roof rising to 2.55, stepping down to the rear box roof at 2.2, and following the rear box down to its base — checking that this sequence of points forms a simple, non-self-intersecting outline.

I'm laying out the full closed polygon as a list of (z,y) coordinates tracing around the hull from the rear base, along the bottom, up the wheel arches, across the front bumper, up the nose, over the windscreen, across the cab roof, down to the rear box, and back to the start. For the windscreen glass, I'm figuring out how to represent it as a thin rotated box tilted to match the slope angle between the hood and roof points, working out the rotation needed around the X axis so the panel's long axis aligns with that incline.

Instead I'll use a plane facing the normal direction with a reflective texture for the windscreen glass, applying it across the box faces for the neon streak effect.

Checking the body dimensions now: wheels centered at x=±1.0 with width 0.45 sit within the arch slot cut through the body, so they stay tucked inside without poking through the sides.

I'm widening the body to 2.4 (x ±1.2) and nudging the wheel centers to ±1.03, so the outer face lands nearly flush with the body side. Since the arch slot cuts all the way through the body width, I need a liner box inside each arch so you don't see straight through to the opposite wheel from the side view.

Checking the gap above the wheel top near the arch roof, I realize a single centered liner box spanning roughly ±0.75 in x is wide enough to block the view-through from both the left and right side angles at once, so I can use one shared blocker instead of two separate ones.

Now I'm fleshing out the add-on body details that increase part count: painting the lower sill region dark for an armored look, adding raised armor plate strips on the flanks between the wheels, and building door assemblies with slim armored window slits and hinge geometry positioned along the cab sides.

Then I'm layering in the front-end details — a heavy push-bar bumper with chevron hazard texture, glowing LED headlight strips, a dark mesh grille, a license plate, a front hood emblem, and neon magenta/cyan underglow and light bars with a roof-mounted strobe beacon — before starting on the rotating base ring for the water cannon turret.

Now I'm building out the water cannon: a rotating housing, a flared nozzle barrel with a glowing cyan core, a hose reel feeding from the tank, plus secondary bumper-mounted spray nozzles. For the tank itself I'm using a lathed cylindrical body with domed ends, decal textures reading "H2O // CROWD DISPERSAL UNIT," a glowing level gauge strip, strap rings, and a ladder, and now I'm moving on to the rear double-door details.

Now I'm adding the rear doors with hinge joints, a riot-shield rack, red neon tail lights, hazard chevron texture, a rear camera, bumper, mud flaps, and step. On the roof I'm placing LRAD-style loudspeaker horns, antennas, a camera dome, searchlights, a cage, and a floodlight rail, while the side panel gets a corporate logo decal, serial number, "SECURITY" lettering, a cyan sill strip with underglow, and a small holographic ad screen.

I'm adding an LED message board above the windshield and another on the rear scrolling "DISPERSE. YOU HAVE 30 SECONDS TO COMPLY," plus matching displays on the sides. For the textures I'm inventing a corporate brand ("TRIGEN Public Order") with a hexagonal triangle emblem logo, and I'm starting on the windscreen texture next.

Still planning more textures: hazard chevron stripes for the bumper and rear, the LED board text, a "TRIGEN // CROWD CONTROL" door decal projected onto the body surface, a tank label, a mesh grille texture with cyan highlights, and I'm considering whether the front should have a face-like arrangement instead of separate headlight/taillight parts.

I'm sketching the front as angry visor-style lights with angular slit headlights and a scanning red strip, plus a number plate texture and wheel hub detailing with eight spokes, along with warning stripes overall. For paints I'm thinking dark grainy tire rubber, scratched steel using mottle-based grime effects imported from the SDK, and a flat cyberpunk corporate color palette of white/graphite with yellow accents.

I'm settling on a hull colorway of white-graphite with navy, yellow accent "#fcee0a", neon cyan and magenta highlights, red taillights, and warning orange. For wheels I'm planning cylindrical tires, eight-sided rims, hubs, lug nuts arranged in a ring, brake discs, and a glowing cyan neon ring per wheel, budgeting around 9 parts per wheel across six wheels while keeping total part count in a reasonable 180-340 range.

Rather than modeling individual lug nuts, I'm switching to a cheaper approach: drawing a rim face texture via an outward-facing circle geometry with spokes and lug dots baked into an SVG texture, reducing each wheel's hub detail to a single textured disc part. Now I'm moving on to suspension components -- axle rods, differential housing as a sphere, and drive shafts.

For steering, I'm setting up a steerFL joint parented to the chassis with wheelFL parented to that, using a Y-direction for the steering pivot and an X-aligned direction for the wheel spin axis along the axle. I'm also considering undercarriage details like a skid plate, frame rails, and an exhaust stack, while checking which bone roles are valid for the wheel joints since "hinge" may not be an allowed role name.

Now I'm laying out the full joint hierarchy: chassis as root, steering and wheel joints on each side, door hinges at the front and rear edges positioned with Y-axis pivots, and turret yaw/pitch joints near the top, working through how the bone direction for the pitch joint should relate to the barrel so rotation happens about the correct axis rather than causing an unwanted roll.

I'm also sketching smaller static details like beacon spin joints on the roof lightbar, keeping the total joint count around twenty, and reviewing the SDK's part/rod/spike/extrude/lathe/sweep/decal function signatures so I use the correct parameters when writing the actual construction code.

Writing geometry helper functions...

For textured planes I'm setting up a part call with position, direction, axis, texture, and bone parameters, plus a glow variant that uses the texture as emissive. I'm also checking how the default up-vector assumption interacts with a plane facing along the z-axis.

For a plane facing straight up or down the orientation becomes degenerate, so I need to pass an explicit up vector in that case. Now I'm working through the orientation math for a plane facing +X, like the model's left flank, computing the viewer's right vector from the facing and up directions to figure out which way the drawing's texture should read.

For the right flank the same logic applies with the direction mirrored. For decals, I'm noting that `b.decal(body, tex, {at, dir, size})` applies texture to a target surface with a small default lift and alpha-tested transparency, useful for flank livery, logos, door numbers, and hood emblems.

Since the hood's slope is nearly flat, the up-vector needs to be set explicitly (like [0,0,1]) rather than relying on world-up, since a near-parallel dir/up pair would degenerate the projection. Given the hood's short 0.75m slope, I'll keep any hood logo small, around 0.5x0.5, and start specifying flank decal placement points on the body surface.

Now I'm working out the livery paint function: lower body graphite dark with accent lines, a thin yellow stripe band where side normals are strong, white upper body with a faint cyan gradient, light grey grime-streaked roof where the normal points up, and bottom grime plus water streaks for wear, all blended into a final mixed color.

For the body panels I'm applying the panelled texture kit with specific size, aspect, and rivet parameters on top of the livery paint, using default ink seams, and making sure unused extrude parameters are prefixed with underscores to satisfy the typechecker. Then I'm setting up the roof light bar housing as a dark box with lens segments split into different glowing colors on each side, using emissive glow for the neon lens strips.

Now I'm working out the water cannon placement on the cab roof—figuring out the yaw and pitch joint positions, barrel length and rotation range so it doesn't collide with the tank behind it, and sizing the drum cylinder base that sits at the turret mount.

Adding reinforcement rings with chevron stripes, plus a sagging hose sweep connecting the tank front to the breech.

I'm adding a magenta-glowing camera pod with a thin cyan laser sight, and reusing the clockwork gauge texture on the tank front and turret housing for extra detail. Now I'm defining the tank's lathed profile points for its body shape.

Working out the saddle height and tank center position so the roof and supports line up correctly—settling on a center y around 3.02 given the radius and saddle offsets.

For the tank's paint, I'm planning a custom shader-like paint function giving it a shiny blue-grey metal look with horizontal stripe bands for a visual accent.

I want to add a decal label on the tank sides reading something like "H₂O // CROWD DISPERSAL // PRESSURE 40 BAR", plus a small sight-glass tube mounted along the tank's rear flank to act as a level gauge.

For structure, I realize the default torus orientation lies flat in the XY plane with its normal along Z, which happens to match the tank's own axis -- so I can place strap rings directly around the tank at several z positions without any extra rotation, using dark steel coloring. Then I'll add box saddles beneath the tank for support, and work on the rear compartment: a pair of doors on the rear face with hazard chevron panels on the lower half, handles, hinge pins, and vertical red glowing tail-light strips along the outer edges.

Now I'm detailing the rear doors as hinged assemblies at the outer edges, each made of a door box with livery coloring, a chevron pattern plane, a handle rod, and maybe a small armored porthole window with a magenta glow. I'm adding a rear bumper/step with mud flaps, a tow hitch, and a textured license plate plane, then moving to the cab's side doors -- building door panels, window openings, and tinted armored glass panes with diagonal highlight textures and bar overlays positioned along the body sides.

Now I'm layering on the window frame (a darker box behind the glass plane), door handles, hinge pin cylinders, door numbering, side mirrors with arm, housing, orange turn-signal glow, and a camera near the A-pillar, plus glowing neon underglow strips along the sills and beltline in cyan and magenta using a helper function for glowing rod segments, and I'm starting on raised armor panels with rivets and a logo decal for the rear flank.

I'm working out the "TRIGEN" decal placement so the text reads correctly left-to-right on both sides of the vehicle, accounting for how the viewer's perspective flips direction depending on which flank they're facing -- deciding not to mirror the text so it reads naturally like real truck lettering. Then I'm moving to the roof details: a light bar with a base box and lens segments, plus a bracket mounting two large sonic emitter horns.

I'm placing those LRAD horns on either side of the roof between the turret and windscreen, defining their lathe profile for the bell shape and giving the interior a subtle magenta glow. I'm also adding a sensor dome on the cab roof, a pair of whip antennas with orange tips, a flat antenna panel, floodlights at the roof's front corners, and figuring out where to mount an LED message board near the light bar.

Now I'm reconsidering placement for that LED board since the rear compartment roof is too shallow -- I'm thinking of inset screens on the flanks of the rear box above the arch slots instead, roughly centered in the body panel between y 1.3 and 2.1.

I'll allocate that flank region to hold a "TRIGEN" decal, a smaller LED glow board, a hex logo decal, and "PUBLIC ORDER DIVISION" text beneath, all via decals and a glow plane. Then I'll move to the front, starting with the push bar bumper built from an extruded chevron profile.

For the bumper, I'm planning a simple box up front with a chevron texture plane on its face, angled end-wrap boxes at the corners, and a riot-style pusher plate shaped as a trapezoid outline extruded forward, basically a flat shield with a rubber bumper strip rather than spikes.

I'm scaling the pusher down to a lower band only, leaving a mesh grille zone above it, and adding four small nozzle cylinders onto the pusher for water/tear-gas ports. I'm also planning angular headlight housings at the ends with glowing cyan slit strips.

Now I'm laying out the full front face vertically: pusher from 0.55–1.2, grille from 1.25–1.65, headlights flanking at the sides, and a slim magenta neon visor bar across the top edge with a hex logo emblem centered in the grille.

Moving to the hood, I'm sloping it from the grille back toward the windscreen, adding intake vents, wiper rods, and an armor ridge, plus an angled shutter plate above the windscreen framed by side pillars. I'm also planning the cabin roof hatch with handrails and the underside details like the skid plate, driveshaft, and axle rods.

Now adding dual exhaust stacks clamped to the rear cab flanks on both sides, running from mid-height up to roof level with clamp rings and a heat shield, keeping the part count tight around fifteen pieces.

Skipping extra fuel tanks under the arch, adding sill steps and textured outer wheel faces, and considering a coiled hose reel on the rear flank—maybe a drum with torus rings mounted near the rear bumper.

Deciding rear-mounted hose reel is awkward since doors are there, so I'll skip it, keeping part count around 250-300. I'm tempted by a stylized cyan water jet arc from the nozzle for visual flair but wary of transparency rules and added complexity, so I'll likely leave it out.

I'm leaning toward cyberpunk flavor text instead: a corporate slogan like "STABILITY IS A SERVICE" and a magenta "CAUTION: LIQUID FORCE" decal as SVG text elements, plus a small glowing burst at the nozzle tip. Now I'm planning the texture list: a hex-shaped "TRIGEN" logo emblem with cyan glow, yellow/black caution chevrons, and a windscreen glass texture...

Still writing texture SVGs...

Importing the glow, panelled, and gaugeTexture kit modules, then double-checking that mix, noise, smoothstep, and paint are actually exported from the main SDK module before relying on them.

Still defining color branches...

Still shaping panel colors...

Writing extrusion code...

Defining more joints...

Still writing wheel geometry...

Still building wheel/axle setup...

Setting up the TRIGEN interceptor module and basic geometry helpers...

Writing SVG logo markup...
